AverageLMC/Assumptions.lean.title: The exact potential and average smoothness constants
AverageLMC/Assumptions.lean.summary: This module represents the paper's state space by EuclideanSpace over Fin p. Every derivative and smoothness constant is computed from one real-valued potential. Coordinate smoothness uses the literal supremum of the Taylor quotients in (coordM); it is not a supplied error bound. The deterministic results assume differentiability and a Lipschitz gradient, without adding a Hessian or third derivative assumption.

steps.title: Euclidean coordinates and literal Taylor quotients
steps.body: State p is the real Euclidean space of dimension p and coordinateVector j is its jth unit vector. The coordinate Taylor quotient is twice the difference between f(x+a e_j) and its first order approximation at x, divided by a squared. The defining set ranges over every x and every nonzero real a. Its supremum is exactly M_j, and the average of these p constants is M_av. A displacement a=1 at x=0 proves that every coordinate quotient set is nonempty. The unit norm and coordinate inner-product identities connect these definitions to Euclidean calculus.

steps.title: The actual global gradient seminorm
steps.body: globalSmoothness is the supremum of the gradient difference norm divided by the state difference norm over unequal states. For p positive, a pair consisting of zero and one coordinate vector witnesses nonemptiness. Any supplied gradient Lipschitz constant M bounds every quotient, so it bounds the supremum. The quotients are nonnegative, hence the supremum is nonnegative. Conversely, each quotient is at most this bounded supremum. Multiplying by the strictly positive state difference norm proves that the gradient is Lipschitz with its exact seminorm. Thus subsequent inequalities may use the literal constant in the paper instead of an arbitrary larger bound.

steps.title: Bound and attain the coordinate quadratic model
steps.body: The shared differentiable descent lemma gives an upper quadratic model with coefficient M/2. At a coordinate displacement a e_j, the inner product is a times the jth gradient coordinate and the squared displacement norm is a squared. For nonzero a, multiply the upper model by 2 and divide by a squared to show that every Taylor quotient is at most M. This proves boundedness of the quotient set and M_j at most M. Each quotient is also at most its supremum M_j. Multiplication by a squared and rearrangement recover the sharper coordinate upper model with coefficient M_j/2. The zero displacement follows directly. No existence of a second derivative is needed.

steps.title: Compare strong convexity, average smoothness and global smoothness
steps.body: The strong-convexity lower model at zero and e_j gives the same first order term as the coordinate upper model, with quadratic coefficients m/2 and M_j/2 respectively. Subtraction yields m at most M_j. Summing the upper and lower bounds over the p coordinates and dividing by positive p proves m at most M_av at most M. Apply the upper bounds to the actual nonnegative global gradient seminorm, using its proved Lipschitz property, to obtain M_j at most M_infinity and M_av at most M_infinity with exactly the paper's supremum constants.

steps.title: Actual Hessian, Laplacian and finite-sum notation
steps.body: hessian is the second Frechet derivative evaluated on pairs of coordinate vectors, and laplacian is mathlib's Laplacian. Expanding the Laplacian in the canonical orthonormal basis gives exactly the matrix trace of this Hessian. LaplacianSmooth records three continuous derivatives and the displayed bound on the squared norm of the gradient of the Laplacian, with the factor p from (lip:2). It does not introduce a Hessian Lipschitz requirement. Finally, rmsComponentSmoothness is the square root of the average of the squared exact component-gradient seminorms, as in (eq:Mtwo).

AverageLMC/GradientStep.lean.title: The deterministic gradient-step and descent lemmas
AverageLMC/GradientStep.lean.summary: The two estimates here concern the actual gradient of the potential. The first uses only strong convexity and differentiability, and the second uses only differentiability and a Lipschitz gradient. Both are proved on arbitrary real Hilbert spaces and therefore apply to the paper's Euclidean space. The proofs also cover the zero step size.

steps.title: The gradient-step lemma (eq:basic-gd)
steps.body: Expand the squared distance after the deterministic gradient step: the result is the original squared distance minus twice h times the inner product of the displacement and the gradient, plus h squared times the squared gradient norm. The supporting-plane inequality for m-strong convexity bounds the negative inner product by f(y)-f(theta) minus m/2 times the squared displacement norm. Multiply that inequality by the nonnegative scalar 2h and substitute it in the expansion. Collecting the squared-distance coefficients gives 1-mh, precisely the paper's displayed gradient-step lemma.

steps.title: Deterministic descent in the smoothing lemma (eq:exp-upper)
steps.body: Apply the shared quadratic upper model for a differentiable potential with M-Lipschitz gradient at the point theta-h times its gradient. Its first order term is minus h times the squared gradient norm, and the quadratic remainder is M h squared/2 times that norm. Multiply by two and factor to obtain minus h times (2-hM) times the squared gradient norm. If hM is at most 2, this right side is nonpositive, which proves that the gradient step does not increase the potential. This verifies the deterministic conclusion of the paper's smoothing lemma; it does not assert the separate expectation inequality for random noise.

AverageLMC/Recurrence.lean.title: Exact scalar contraction and recurrence iteration
AverageLMC/Recurrence.lean.summary: Write \(r_k=(m/p)W_2^2(\nu_k,\pi)\), \(t=mh\), and \(a=\kappa_{\mathrm{av}}+1\) when the dimension is positive. This module proves implications for arbitrary real sequences satisfying the displayed scalar recurrence. It does not construct an LMC law, establish its Wasserstein one-step inequality, or infer that inequality from convexity and smoothness. Its constant-step conclusion is the scalar arithmetic underlying Theorem 1; its harmonic induction is the decreasing-step calculation in Proposition 1.

steps.title: Bound the rational contraction by the exponential
steps.body: For \(0\le t\le1\), prove \[(1-t)/(1+t)\le e^{-2t}.\] At the endpoint \(t=1\), the left side is zero and the exponential is positive. For \(t<1\), both \(1-t\) and \(1+t\) are positive. The first term of the established logarithmic series lower bound gives \[t\le\tfrac12\log\frac{1+t}{1-t}.\] Since the two rational fractions are reciprocals, their logarithms have opposite signs. Thus \(\log((1-t)/(1+t))\le-2t\); monotonicity of the exponential proves the desired estimate. The proof handles \(t=0\) directly within the non-strict branch, so no positive-step assumption is added.

steps.title: Iterate an affine inequality up to a finite horizon
steps.body: Let \(q\ge0\) and \(c\ge0\). If \(r_{j+1}\le q r_j+(1-q)c\) is known only for \(j<n\), induction proves the stronger finite-horizon identity-shaped bound \[r_k\le q^k r_0+(1-q^k)c\qquad(0\le k\le n).\] The successor proof multiplies the preceding bound by nonnegative \(q\), inserts the one-step assumption, and expands \(q^{k+1}=q^kq\). Since \(q^nc\ge0\), discarding the correction \(-q^nc\) yields \(r_n\le q^nr_0+c\). No contraction condition \(q<1\) is needed for this algebraic statement. The finite-horizon hypothesis is essential for the warmup application, where the schedule changes after a prescribed time.

steps.title: Resolve the constant-step recurrence with the paper's bias constant
steps.body: Assume \(a\ge0\), \(0\le t\le1\), \(r_0\ge0\), and \[r_{j+1}\le\frac{1-t}{1+t}r_j+\frac{at^2}{1+t}.\] Put \(q=(1-t)/(1+t)\) and \(c=at/2\). Positive \(1+t\) makes \(q\ge0\), and rational algebra gives exactly \[\frac{at^2}{1+t}=(1-q)\frac{at}{2}.\] Apply the finite-horizon affine lemma. Raising the previously proved inequality \(q\le e^{-2t}\) to the natural power \(n\), and using \((e^{-2t})^n=e^{-2tn}\), bounds the initial-error contribution. Its multiplication by \(r_0\) uses the explicit nonnegativity hypothesis. Therefore \[r_n\le e^{-2tn}r_0+\frac{at}{2}.\] The first declaration assumes the recurrence only before \(n\); the second specializes it to a recurrence valid at every natural time. In unnormalized paper notation the bias equals \((M_{\mathrm{av}}+m)hp/(2m)\). This interpretation is an algebraic substitution, not a proved stochastic endpoint in these files.

steps.title: Close the decreasing-step induction exactly
steps.body: For \(x\ge1\), the coefficient \(q_x=(1-1/x)/(1+1/x)\) is nonnegative. Hence \(r\le a/x\) implies \[q_xr+\frac{a/x^2}{1+1/x}\le q_x\frac ax+\frac{a/x^2}{1+1/x}=\frac a{x+1}.\] The equality follows by clearing the positive denominators and expanding products. The local lemma does not require \(a\ge0\). For the tail theorem, let \(\kappa\ge1\), initialize \(r_0\le a/\kappa\), and assume the given recurrence uses \(t_n=1/(\kappa+n)\). Natural induction applies the local lemma at \(x=\kappa+n\), proving \[r_n\le\frac a{\kappa+n}.\] The tail theorem retains \(a\ge0\), consistent with \(a=\kappa_{\mathrm{av}}+1\). This conclusion is conditional on the scalar recurrence; it does not supply its analytic source.

AverageLMC/Complexity.lean.title: Proposition 1: scalar warmup, variable steps and iteration count
AverageLMC/Complexity.lean.summary: Use \(a=\kappa_{\mathrm{av}}+1>0\), \(\kappa=\kappa_{\max}\ge1\), and \(\varepsilon_0>0\). The paper's exact positive logarithm, warmup ceiling, decreasing-step schedule and accuracy ceiling are represented explicitly. Given \(0\le r_0\le\varepsilon_0^2\) and the normalized scalar one-step recurrence, the module proves \(r_k\le a/(\kappa+k-k_0)\) for \(k\ge k_0\), then \(r_k\le\varepsilon^2\) at the stated iteration count. All stochastic, coupling and Wasserstein facts needed to establish that recurrence remain external proof obligations.

steps.title: Encode the exact positive logarithm and two-phase schedule
steps.body: The definitions are \[\log_+(z)=\max\{\log z,0\},\qquad k_0=\left\lceil\frac\kappa2\log_+\!\left(\frac{2\kappa\varepsilon_0^2}{a}\right)\right\rceil,\qquad t_k=\frac1{\kappa+(k-k_0)_+}.\] In Lean, the ceiling is a natural-number ceiling and \((k-k_0)_+\) is represented by subtraction in the natural numbers, cast afterward to \(\mathbb R\). Thus the difference is exactly zero before warmup ends; for \(k\ge k_0\) it is the ordinary integer difference. The dimensionless step \(t_k=mh_k\) corresponds to the paper's \(h_k=1/(M_{\max}+m(k-k_0)_+)\). These are definitions, with no hidden decay or convergence assumptions.

steps.title: Verify the smoothness restriction for the full schedule
steps.body: For \(\kappa>0\), the cast natural difference is nonnegative, so \(\kappa+(k-k_0)_+\ge\kappa>0\). Positivity of the reciprocal and monotonicity of reciprocals give \[0<t_k\le1/\kappa.\] When \(\kappa=\kappa_{\max}=M_{\max}/m\), this is the arithmetic behind \(h_kM_{\max}\le1\). It verifies the schedule's restriction for every step, including those in the warmup phase; it does not assert the one-step stochastic inequality itself.

steps.title: Use the warmup ceiling to reduce the initial error
steps.body: Let \(R=2\kappa\varepsilon_0^2/a>0\). The natural ceiling gives \[k_0\ge\frac\kappa2\max\{\log R,0\}\ge\frac\kappa2\log R.\] Multiplying and dividing by the positive \(\kappa\) yields \(-2k_0/\kappa\le-\log R\). Exponentiate this inequality and multiply by the nonnegative \(\varepsilon_0^2\): \[e^{-2k_0/\kappa}\varepsilon_0^2\le e^{-\log R}\varepsilon_0^2=\frac a{2\kappa}.\] The final equality uses \(e^{\log R}=R\) on its verified positive domain and cancels nonzero parameters. The same proof covers \(R\le1\), where the positive logarithm is zero and the warmup length can vanish.

steps.title: Join warmup to the harmonic tail
steps.body: Assume \(0\le r_0\le\varepsilon_0^2\) and, for every natural \(k\), \[r_{k+1}\le\frac{1-t_k}{1+t_k}r_k+\frac{at_k^2}{1+t_k},\qquad t_k=\frac1{\kappa+(k-k_0)_+}.\] Before \(k_0\), natural subtraction gives \(t_k=1/\kappa\). The finite-horizon constant-step theorem therefore gives \[r_{k_0}\le e^{-2k_0/\kappa}r_0+\frac a{2\kappa}\le\frac a\kappa,\] where the second inequality uses the initialization bound and the warmup-decay lemma. Shift the sequence to \(s_n=r_{k_0+n}\). Cancellation of the natural subtraction gives \(t_{k_0+n}=1/(\kappa+n)\), so the harmonic tail theorem applies and proves \(s_n\le a/(\kappa+n)\). For any \(k\ge k_0\), choose \(n=k-k_0\) and use \(k_0+(k-k_0)=k\), obtaining \[r_k\le\frac a{\kappa+(k-k_0)}.\] This is precisely the scalar calculation in the proof of Proposition 1, with the recurrence kept as an explicit hypothesis rather than disguised as a convexity or smoothness assumption.

steps.title: Verify the accuracy ceiling and conclude the conditional rate
steps.body: The exact iteration threshold is \[k_\varepsilon=k_0+\left\lceil\max\left\{\frac a{\varepsilon^2}-\kappa,0\right\}\right\rceil.\] Suppose \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(k\ge k_\varepsilon\). Natural arithmetic first gives \(k\ge k_0\) and then bounds \(k-k_0\) below by that ceiling. After casting to \(\mathbb R\), \[k-k_0\ge\max\{a/\varepsilon^2-\kappa,0\}\ge a/\varepsilon^2-\kappa.\] Thus \(\kappa+(k-k_0)\ge a/\varepsilon^2\). Both denominators used in rearrangement are positive, proving \[\frac a{\kappa+(k-k_0)}\le\varepsilon^2.\] The arithmetic envelope theorem proves this implication without a recurrence. The final accuracy theorem combines it with the preceding conditional scalar Proposition 1 to obtain \(r_k\le\varepsilon^2\). It proves no independent assertion that actual LMC errors obey the required recurrence.

AverageLMC/GLMObstruction.lean.title: An explicit obstruction to the isotropic GLM Hessian estimate
AverageLMC/GLMObstruction.lean.summary:
The isotropic row of the paper's GLM proposition asserts a Hessian operator-norm Lipschitz bound of order n, with a multiplicative constant depending only on the component derivative bound C_g. This module checks a permitted family with one component g_1(t)=t squared minus sin(t) and every other component equal to t squared. It identifies the actual finite-sum potential, its gradient and its Hessian, and proves that every Hessian Lipschitz constant must be at least the cube of the first design vector's norm. The Gaussian probability argument is proved separately. These are checked obstruction ingredients, not proofs of the paper's convergence theorems.

The fixed component family is \(g_1(t)=t^2-\sin t\), \(g_i(t)=t^2\) for \(i\ne1\). Its actual Hessian is \[H(x)=Q+\sin\langle a,x\rangle\,aa^\top,\qquad Q=2\sum_iX_iX_i^\top.\] Every operator norm Lipschitz bound M for H satisfies \(\|a\|^3\le M\).

steps.title: The oscillating component and its actual derivatives
steps.body: Define g(t)=t squared minus sin(t), g'(t)=2t minus cos(t), and g''(t)=2 plus sin(t). Differentiate these formulas using the power and trigonometric derivative rules; the third derivative is cos(t). These are derivatives of the same component, rather than independently supplied derivative fields. Polynomial and sine functions are smooth on the whole real line, so this choice satisfies the component regularity in the manuscript.

steps.title: A fixed derivative bound independent of dimension
steps.body: The inequality sin(t) at least minus one gives g''(t) at least one. Therefore g'' is nonnegative and its absolute value is itself. The bounds sin(t) at most one and absolute cos(t) at most one yield absolute g''(t) plus absolute g'''(t) at most four, uniformly over t. The component selector uses this oscillating function at the distinguished index and the quadratic at every other index. Each quadratic has second derivative two and third derivative zero. The module proves smoothness, convexity and the bound on actual second and third derivatives for every selected component. Thus the same fixed C_g=4 applies to every component in every dimension.

steps.title: Write the finite-sum potential and its score explicitly
steps.body: For a finite design family X_i and a distinguished index i_0, the potential is the sum of the squared inner products with X_i, minus one copy of sin of the inner product with X_i0. Expanding the selector and summing the unique sine correction proves that this is exactly the GLM sum with the certified component family. Its smoothness on the whole state space follows from finite sums and composition of smooth polynomials, linear functionals and sine. Its constant quadratic Hessian Q is twice the sum of the rank-one operators X_i X_i transpose. The score is Qx minus cos of the inner product with a times a, where a=X_i0. Differentiate each squared linear functional, sum the resulting continuous linear derivatives, and subtract the derivative of the single sine term. The result is the inner-product functional represented by this explicit score.

steps.title: Differentiate the score to obtain the Hessian
steps.body: Differentiate Qx using the constant linear map Q. The derivative of the negative cosine term is sin of the inner product with a times the rank-one operator aa transpose. Thus the Hessian is H(x)=Q plus sin of the inner product with a times aa transpose. This formula is proved as the Frechet derivative of the explicit score. In a complete real inner-product space, the previously proved derivative of the potential identifies this score as its actual gradient. Taking that gradient's derivative then identifies H as the actual Hessian. The operator norm used for these continuous linear maps is exactly the Euclidean operator norm relevant to the manuscript's M_2.

steps.title: Differentiate the Hessian along the design direction
steps.body: Restrict the Hessian to the path x=t a. Its sine coefficient becomes sin(t times the squared norm of a). At t=0 this scalar function has derivative equal to the squared norm of a. Consequently the derivative of H(t a) at zero is the squared norm of a times the rank-one operator aa transpose. The rank-one operator has norm equal to the squared norm of a, so the Hessian path derivative has norm equal to the fourth power of the norm of a.

steps.title: Every Hessian Lipschitz constant has cubic growth
steps.body: Suppose H is M-Lipschitz in operator norm, with M nonnegative. Along x=t a, the path is M times the norm of a Lipschitz, because its state displacement has norm absolute t times the norm of a. A derivative of a Lipschitz path has norm at most its Lipschitz constant. The preceding derivative calculation therefore gives the fourth power of the norm of a at most M times the norm of a. If a is nonzero, divide by its positive norm to obtain the cube of its norm at most M. If a is zero, the result follows from M nonnegative. With n=p and a standard Gaussian first design vector, the separate Gaussian module shows why this necessary cubic lower bound prevents a uniform order-n bound with probability one half.

AverageLMC/GaussianObstruction.lean.title: The actual Gaussian norm probability obstruction
AverageLMC/GaussianObstruction.lean.summary: This module uses the actual standard Gaussian measure in dimension p, with no assumed concentration event. It proves the exact variance of its squared norm and rules out a dimension independent order-p bound on its cubed norm with probability one half. This is the probability ingredient for the GLM counterexample.

steps.title: Compute the squared-norm variance from exact Gaussian moments
steps.body: The standard Gaussian second moment is \(p\), and the shared fourth-moment theorem gives \(p^2+2p\). Gaussian integrability of every finite moment proves square integrability of the squared norm before using the variance formula. Subtracting the squared mean gives \(\operatorname{Var}(\|Z\|^2)=2p\). Thus no finite-moment premise is supplied externally.

steps.title: Apply Chebyshev to the small-norm event
steps.body: If \(\|Z\|^2<p/2\), its deviation from its mean p is at least p/2. Chebyshev bounds the probability by \(2p/(p/2)^2=8/p\). The proof uses a set inclusion and the actual Gaussian law, retaining the extended nonnegative probability values.

steps.title: Disprove every uniform cubic norm bound
steps.body: Let \(C\ge0\) and \(p>8C^2\). If \(\|Z\|^2\ge p/2\), then \(\|Z\|^6\ge p^3/8>C^2p^2\), so \(\|Z\|^3>Cp\). Therefore the event \(\|Z\|^3\le Cp\) is contained in the small-norm event. When also \(p>16\), its probability is at most \(8/p<1/2\). For every proposed C choose a natural dimension larger than both thresholds; its probability contradicts the proposed universal one-half lower bound.

AverageLMC/GLMCounterexample.lean.title: A Gaussian-design counterexample using the actual potential Hessian
AverageLMC/GLMCounterexample.lean.summary: This module combines the genuine finite-sum GLM potential and the Gaussian probability obstruction. The design has n=p independent standard Gaussian rows, exactly the isotropic case allowed by the source. The bound event uses the derivative of the actual gradient of the actual potential, so no Hessian identification or concentration estimate is assumed.

steps.title: Construct precisely the square isotropic Gaussian design
steps.body: GaussianDesign p stores p vectors in \(\mathbb R^p\). Its measure is the finite product of p standard Gaussian laws. The product is a probability measure; evaluation at any row preserves the standard Gaussian law, and the coordinate evaluation maps are independent. These facts establish the design assumptions for the counterexample.

steps.title: Translate the table into an actual Hessian event
steps.body: The isotropic table asserts \(M_2\sqrt p\le Cn\sqrt p\), so at n=p it requires the actual Hessian to be Lipschitz with bound Cp. glmHessianBoundEvent expresses exactly that inequality for all states using fderiv of the actual gradient. The proved rank-one lower bound forces every design in this event to satisfy \(\|X_i\|^3\le Cp\). The row law transfers this event probability to the standard Gaussian measure. For \(p>16\) and \(p>8C^2\), the probability is strictly below one half.

steps.title: Rule out every dimension independent table constant
steps.body: Assume one nonnegative constant C makes the Hessian bound event have probability at least one half for every positive dimension. Choose a natural p above both 16 and \(8C^2\); the previous theorem gives probability below one half for its first row, a contradiction. The component derivative bound is always the fixed value four, so allowing C to depend only on that bound does not remove the contradiction. The full-paper convergence claims remain separate unproved requirements.

AverageLMC.lean.title: Average smoothness: checked components and the source obstruction
AverageLMC.lean.summary: This import bundle gathers exact deterministic lemmas, conditional scalar recurrence bounds, and an actual-potential Gaussian-design counterexample. It is explicitly an incomplete paper formalization. It does not export a new actual-law LMC or SGLD convergence endpoint.

AverageLMC/Check.lean.title: Audit the logical dependencies of the proved components
AverageLMC/Check.lean.summary: The audit imports the library and prints the axioms used by each central deterministic, scalar and counterexample theorem. Only the standard Lean mathematical foundations are expected. A successful audit does not discharge the unproved stochastic endpoints or certify the false source proposition.
